tldr: In World Action Models (WAMs) that predict future video and robot actions simultaneously, Rolling-WAM distributes the joint denoising computation across successive replanning cycles. While preserving future prediction quality, it dramatically cuts inference latency, achieving a 4.5x speedup over conventional models and high manipulation success rates on a real-world humanoid robot.
hero_caption: Overall framework of Rolling-WAM. In (a), video and action experts are coupled via attention. In (b), rolling inference fully denoises and executes only the imminent action chunk, while partially refining farther-future chunks to carry over to the next cycle. (c) shows the attention mask that shares video context across the entire action horizon while isolating actions from each other.
overview:
World Action Models (WAMs) have attracted significant interest for complex robot manipulation because they predict not only the robot's actions, but also how the environment's visual appearance will change as a result. Acting while imagining future visual outcomes makes them very capable. However, they had a major weakness: inference is extremely computationally heavy. For a robot to react to disturbances and environmental shifts, closed-loop control that updates plans from fresh observations at short intervals is essential. Yet denoising future video and actions from scratch at every cycle with diffusion models takes too long, severely delaying action updates.

To tackle this, the authors drew inspiration from human behavior: humans decide near-future motions specifically, but keep distant future plans as rough assumptions, gradually refining them as the situation unfolds. The proposed method, Rolling-WAM, splits the prediction window into several chunks. It fully denoises the imminent chunk for execution, while holding farther-future chunks at higher noise levels as 'drafts.' When the robot executes the imminent motion and slides the window forward by one step, it brings in new camera observations and continues denoising the carried-over drafts. This spreads the denoising cost over time while keeping an evolving visual-action context to guide action generation.

Evaluations were conducted on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 simulation benchmarks, as well as on a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid robot across three manipulation tasks. Compared to standard joint WAMs that denoise from scratch every cycle, Rolling-WAM achieved a 4.5x steady-state replanning speedup (215 ms per cycle) while matching or exceeding the manipulation success rates of state-of-the-art models.
contributions: Proposed Rolling-WAM, a new World Action Model framework that distributes joint video and action denoising across successive replanning cycles over time.

Formulated a staggered noise schedule that fully denoises only the imminent action for execution while progressively refining the distant future, complete with initialization and rolling operating modes.
Designed a specialized attention structure coupling video and action DiTs, allowing actions to broadly reference future video features while preventing cross-chunk action interference.
Achieved a 4.5x speedup over standard joint WAMs and competitive task success rates in simulation and on a real-world humanoid (Unitree G1), reaching 98.1% on LIBERO and 93.3% on RoboTwin.

sections.heading: Why Do World Action Models Need 'Rolling' Imagination?
sections.summary: While World Action Models predicting future video and actions simultaneously are promising, denoising everything from scratch at every cycle introduces large latency and degrades closed-loop responsiveness. Rolling-WAM solves this by spreading the denoising process across multiple cycles, fully refining only the imminent action for execution.
sections.details:
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach for flexible robotic manipulation by predicting future observation video alongside robot action outputs. Forecasting the future visual scene provides rich environmental context to the action generator, which is their greatest advantage.

However, operating in the real world requires closed-loop control (Receding Horizon Control), where the robot regularly incorporates new observations to correct its trajectory. In standard WAMs, each replanning cycle requires evaluating the diffusion model repeatedly to denoise the entire prediction horizon from pure Gaussian noise into clean predictions. This heavy iterative computation creates latency, hindering the robot's responsiveness. Some prior works speed this up by skipping video generation at test time, but that discards the very future visual prediction intended to support action generation.

The authors identified a clear computational inefficiency in conventional approaches. Even when a long future horizon is fully denoised at every cycle, the robot only executes the earliest action chunk, and the remaining unexecuted predictions are discarded in the next cycle. If those unexecuted predictions could be carried forward rather than thrown away, and gradually refined as new observations arrive, the denoising steps needed in any single cycle could be dramatically reduced.

This insight led to Rolling-WAM. The prediction horizon is partitioned into multiple chunks. The imminent chunk is fully denoised for execution, while subsequent chunks are kept with staggered, higher noise levels. With each window shift, predictions carried over from the prior cycle are further refined, and a fresh noise chunk is appended at the tail. This preserves full future imagination while delivering a 4.5x steady-state replanning speedup.

sections.heading: Differences from Prior Work: A New Path Neither Omitting Nor Caching Video Predictions
sections.summary: Prior efforts to accelerate World Action Models relied on omitting video prediction, feature caching, or distillation. Unlike these, Rolling-WAM distributes the joint video-action denoising process itself across the time axis, utilizing an evolving future prediction for action generation.
sections.details:
To understand where this work fits, let us look at three related research lines.

### II-A World Action Models for Robot Manipulation
Early research estimated actions conditioned on future video plans generated from language instructions. More recently, methods have emerged that jointly model video and actions using pretrained video generation backbones. However, iteratively denoising both video and actions simultaneously is computationally expensive, creating a bottleneck for practical deployment.

### II-B Inference Acceleration for World Action Models
Various attempts have been made to speed up WAM inference. For example, Fast-WAM completely omits future video generation during inference. Other approaches run the video expert pass only once to cache features, or rely on model downsizing and distillation. Some studies partially reuse video features or update them asynchronously. However, these methods either degrade future prediction quality or require complex system pipelines. Rather than stripping away predictions, Rolling-WAM takes a fundamentally different approach by distributing joint video and action denoising across replanning cycles within a sliding window.

### II-C Rolling Diffusion in Sequential Generation
The idea of Rolling Diffusion—advancing denoising with staggered noise levels along a temporal sequence—was originally proposed for autoregressive long video generation. In robotics, Streaming Diffusion Policy similarly accelerated inference by partially denoising an action-only buffer. However, these were restricted to small, action-only models. Rolling-WAM extends this rolling mechanism to coupled world models (video prediction) and action generation for the first time, proving its effectiveness in large-scale multi-task manipulation.

sections.heading: How Rolling-WAM Works: Staggered Noise and a Sliding Window
sections.summary: Rolling-WAM splits the prediction horizon into multiple chunks, fully denoising only the imminent chunk before execution while partially refining the rest. The model couples a pretrained video DiT and an action DiT using a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture, trained in a unified manner with Flow Matching.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation and Computational Bottleneck
At time $t$, the policy receives camera observation $o_t$, robot proprioceptive state $s_t$, and language instruction $\ell$, and predicts an $H$-step action sequence $\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H-1}$. A WAM simultaneously models the corresponding future video latents $\mathbf{v}_{t+1:t+H}$ across the same physical duration. Under standard closed-loop execution, running many denoising steps from pure noise at each replanning cycle incurs substantial latency.

### III-B Rolling Video-Action Denoising
Rolling-WAM partitions the entire prediction window into $W$ chunks $\mathbf{X}_{1:W}$. Each chunk $\mathbf{X}_j = (\mathbf{v}^{(j)}, \mathbf{a}^{(j)})$ contains $K$ action steps and the corresponding video duration, yielding a total prediction horizon of $H=WK$. Inference operates in two modes:

- **Rolling mode (steady state)**: As the progress parameter $\tau$ decreases from $1$ to $0$ across a cycle, the noise level of chunk $j$ transitions along $\sigma( (j-\tau)/W )$. By the end of the cycle, chunk 1 becomes completely clean ($\sigma=0$) and ready for execution, while chunk $j$ reaches the starting noise level of position $j-1$. After execution, chunk 1 is discarded, the window slides by one, and a new pure-noise chunk ($\sigma=1$) is appended at the tail.
- **Initialization mode**: At the start of an episode without past predictions, all chunks begin from pure noise. Noise removal is prioritized for earlier chunks, scheduled so that the final state matches the starting state of Rolling mode.

### III-C Sampling and Execution
Allocating $N$ total denoising steps per chunk, the steps required per cycle in steady state is only $N/W$ (e.g., with $N=10$ and $W=5$, just 2 steps per cycle). By updating the entire window simultaneously with Euler velocity field steps, the robot executes the $K$ actions of chunk 1 while capturing fresh camera observations and transitioning to the next cycle. Distributing computation across time makes it possible to predict far into the future ($WK$) while keeping per-cycle latency minimal.

### III-D Model Architecture and Training Objective
The architecture adopts a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) design combining a pretrained Video Diffusion Transformer (Wan2.2-TI2V-5B) with a lightweight Action Transformer. The attention masking is carefully structured: each action chunk can attend to all video features across the entire window, but direct attention between actions is restricted to the same chunk, and attention from video to action is blocked. This allows actions to leverage a coherent future visual rollout as guidance, without being corrupted by actions from other chunks at different noise levels. The model is trained using Flow Matching with a blend of Rolling mode (0.8 probability) and Initialization mode (0.2 probability), enabling a single model to support both cold starts and steady rolling execution.

captions.F2: Rolling-WAM architecture and inference flow. In (a), the current observation image, text instruction, and robot state are input, and Video DiT and Action DiT collaborate via masked joint attention. In (b), the window slides as the imminent chunk is executed, and the attention mask in (c) allows actions to reference future video predictions across the full horizon.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Significant Speedup and High Success Rates on a Real Humanoid
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Rolling-WAM achieved a 4.5x speedup (215 ms) over standard Joint-WAM, while surpassing baselines with strong manipulation success rates in both simulation and the real world.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations covered three domains: (1) **LIBERO**: 4 suites (40 tasks in total) assessing general manipulation capabilities. (2) **RoboTwin 2.0**: 50 dual-arm manipulation tasks tested in both clean environments and randomized environments with varying backgrounds and objects. (3) **Real-world Unitree G1 humanoid**: Three challenging tasks: toy packaging, stacking 3 plates, and pouring beads. Actions consist of a 64-dimensional whole-body motion latent (SONIC) and 7 dimensions per hand, totaling 78 dimensions, controlled at 10 Hz.

### IV-B Implementation Details
Wan2.2-TI2V-5B was used as the video expert, and a ~1B parameter Transformer as the action expert. Default parameters were set to $W=5$ chunks, $N=10$ total steps, and $K=16$ actions per chunk, resulting in only 2 denoising steps ($10/5=2$) per cycle in steady state.

### IV-C Simulation Benchmark Results
On LIBERO, Rolling-WAM achieved an average success rate of **98.1%**. This is nearly identical to Joint-WAM (98.5%), which runs heavy denoising from scratch every cycle, and outperforms Fast-WAM (97.6%), which omits video generation. On RoboTwin 2.0 with substantial scene variations, it reached 93.5% in clean environments and 93.0% in random environments (average **93.3%**), ranking highest ahead of Joint-WAM (90.6%), Fast-WAM (91.8%), and LingBot-VA (92.2%). Despite using only 2 steady-state steps, progressively refining future context provides noticeable robustness.

### IV-D Inference Efficiency Evaluation
Measuring steady-state replanning latency on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, generating 16 actions took only **215 ms**. This is an **approx. 4.5x** speedup over Joint-WAM's 978 ms, and **approx. 2.5x** over Fast-WAM's 548 ms (which skips video generation). While running faster than leading VLA models like $\pi_{0.5}$ (296 ms) and GR00T N1.7 (285 ms), Rolling-WAM simultaneously predicts and maintains future video up to 80 actions ahead.

### IV-E Real-World Humanoid Evaluation
In real-robot experiments on the Unitree G1, Rolling-WAM achieved an average success rate of **85.0%**, clearly outperforming Joint-WAM (78.3%) and Fast-WAM (75.0%). In particular, it recorded a 70% success rate on bead pouring, which requires delicate adjustments. Long inference pauses in Joint-WAM caused jerky motions and task failures. In contrast, Rolling-WAM moved smoothly and continuously, demonstrating that reducing latency is critical for physical control.

### IV-F Ablation Studies
Varying window size $W$, performance peaked at $W=5$. Extending the window to 8 increased uncertainty about the distant future, confusing imminent actions. Additionally, allowing direct cross-attention between action chunks hurt success rates, confirming the design choice of sharing future visual context while isolating action chunks from one another.

The robot arm motion and drawer opening are faithfully predicted, showing that visual context is maintained without breakdown during rolling execution.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Toward Low-Latency Embodied AI
sections.summary: By distributing denoising computation across multiple cycles, Rolling-WAM achieves a dramatic inference speedup while preserving the prediction quality of World Action Models. Future directions include adaptive window management for sudden environmental changes and asynchronous execution.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Rolling-WAM, an approach that collaboratively refines near- and far-future video and action predictions within a sliding window. It addresses the primary drawback of conventional WAMs—high accuracy at the cost of slow inference—through temporal computational distribution. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and the real-world Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrate that high speed and strong manipulation capability can go hand in hand.

### Limitations and Future Work
The authors highlight several open challenges. First, optimal window and chunk sizes depend on task dynamics and control frequencies, leaving adaptive tuning across environments as future work. Second, because past predictions are retained and shifted forward, unexpected, abrupt changes in the environment may cause retained predictions to diverge from reality and mislead action generation. Developing dynamic window management and asynchronous execution pipelines that fully overlap inference with execution are promising directions to address these limitations.

takeaways: By recognizing that discarding unexecuted future predictions is wasteful, reusing and distributing computation over time achieves a 4.5x inference speedup.
The rolling schedule—fully concretizing the near future while keeping the far future as a draft at higher noise—aligns with human planning intuition and fits robot control naturally.

In action generation, broadly attending to future video features is beneficial, but directly mixing action features across chunks introduces noise conflicts, making isolated action attention essential.
In whole-body control tasks on real humanoids, smooth motion stemming from low inference latency directly impacts task success rates even more than theoretical algorithmic accuracy alone.
limitations: When sudden environmental changes occur (such as abrupt object movements), stale predictions carried over through the sliding window may diverge from reality and mislead action generation.
The optimal window size ($W=5$) and chunk size are currently fixed, lacking dynamic adaptation mechanisms for varying task speeds or control frequencies.
While per-cycle denoising steps are reduced, attention must still be computed over the entire future window at once, requiring substantial GPU memory and parallel compute resources.
